title: Channel Count, Not Horizon Length, Drives Architectural Divergence in Multi-Horizon Urban Growth Prediction
summary: Shows that losing input channels, not lengthening the forecast horizon, drives most of the apparent architectural divergence in urban-growth prediction.
status: Published, sole author. Proceedings of the 1st International Conference on Geospatial Artificial Intelligence, Ghent. PDF is on Zenodo.
abstract: The six-page version of the channel-count audit, presented as an oral at GeoAI 2026 in Ghent. Multi-horizon urban-growth benchmarks keep showing the CNN getting worse as the forecast horizon extends while the ConvLSTM gets better, and the difference gets credited to recurrence. But pushing the horizon out also drops an input epoch, cutting the CNN's input from 24 channels to 21. That lost input accounts for 94% of the CNN's decline (delta-method 95% CI [62%, 100%]). With channels matched, the CNN leads at every horizon, and the ConvLSTM's gain turns out to be positional: removing its most recent epoch moves its score 5.4 times as much as removing the four oldest combined.

title: The Channel-Count Confound: A Continental Audit of Multi-Horizon Urban Growth Prediction
summary: Extended version of the GeoAI paper, with the full ablations and the MC Dropout uncertainty analysis.
status: Accepted, to appear. Sole author. The extended version of the GeoAI paper, with the full ablations and the MC Dropout uncertainty analysis.
abstract: The full audit behind the GeoAI paper, run over 5,698 tiles of the continental US at 250 m with a spatial holdout, a sealed 2020 temporal holdout, and a zero-shot transfer to Lagos. The core finding is the same: the apparent horizon effect in CNN versus ConvLSTM comparisons is mostly an input-design effect, because a longer horizon also means fewer input channels. This version adds the full ablations and the MC Dropout uncertainty analysis over 8.69M pixels, where uncertainty ranks error almost perfectly (r = 0.983) but understates its size by 1.4 to 1.9 times.

title: Confident but Unidentifiable: Positivity Limits on Cross-Region Attribution in Geospatial Models
summary: Derives a positivity diagnostic and partial-identification bound for cross-region attribution; across 44 cities, a confident, well-fit explanation gets the sign of the transfer gap wrong in every degrading model.
abstract: When a geospatial model fails in a new region, people reach for a covariate to blame: the terrain is rougher, the settlement pattern is different. I ask whether that kind of attribution is even identifiable before anyone trusts it. Framed as a transportability problem, the answer is often no. I derive a positivity diagnostic and a partial-identification bound you can compute from the source data alone, including a threshold past which not even the sign of an attribution is recoverable. On land-cover transfer from the contiguous US to 44 cities across four world regions, overlap with the training data drops as low as 5.8%, and a confident, well-fit explanation predicts the wrong sign of the transfer gap in every architecture that actually degrades, which is direct evidence of a regional effect the measured covariates never capture. The point is a reporting standard: an honest geographic explanation should say what it can and cannot identify, not just what it attributes.

title: Understanding Academic Collaboration Networks through Small World Theory
status: Course research project, supervised by Prof. Dana Fine, UMass Dartmouth.
abstract: I built a co-authorship network of 33,981 researchers and 624,928 links from OpenAlex, using the PyAlex library, and tested it against small-world theory. Its clustering coefficient is 0.71, about 650 times that of a random graph with the same density, and the largest connected component holds 61% of the authors.
